meta.case_name: The Run of the Mill NOWOCO

prompt.context: Our client is a Germany-based material manufacturer called 'The Run of the Mill NOWOCO' specializing in a range of products for the construction industry. In recent months, our client has benefited from anti-dumping taxes on the import of similar products. This has resulted in a demand surge for our client and other domestic competitors; however overall profitability is going down and customer complaints about order fulfilment are at an all-time high.
prompt.question: As an integral part of your team, what do you think is going on here? The ultimate goals are to maximize overall profitability and order fulfilment % for key customers.

clarifying_info.q: What products does the client sell?
clarifying_info.a: The client sells products for the construction industry; specific product lines are irrelevant for this case.
It sells directly to customers and through distributors in Germany only.
The client is one of the 3 largest domestic producers with almost 30% market share.
Profitability = Revenue minus Variable Costs (profitability over variable costs).
Order fulfilment % = (% of tons delivered on time) / (total tons ordered).

exhibits.title: Production & Loss Time Info — Utilization & Operational Efficiency at Run of the Mill NOWOCO Plants
exhibits.shows: A chart showing the production time ratio, scheduled loss time ratio, and unscheduled loss time ratio for three plants (Plant A, Plant B, Plant C) versus an industry average benchmark. Total time available = 100%, Production = 82%, Scheduled loss = 10%, Unscheduled loss = 8%.

data.note: Exact per-plant bar values are shown in the chart; all three plants together sum to 100% total utilization.

exhibits.title: Commercial Construction Customer Data
exhibits.shows: A table listing 7 named customers (A through G) plus an 'Others' category, with columns for Revenue (Millions of Euros), Volumes Ordered (thousands of tons), and Order Fulfilment %. A note states that the cost is a constant 1,250 Euros/ton.

framework: Financial aspects: revenues and variable costs — what is driving profitability down despite demand surge
Operational issues: manufacturing utilization, process/lead times, logistics, upstream and downstream constraints
External factors: competitor response, macroeconomic environment, geography

questions.prompt: What are some ways the client can increase order fulfilment, and what are the trade-offs?
questions.guidance: Candidate should brainstorm levers across: (1) reduce process/transportation/lead times, (2) increase inventory levels, (3) more accurate demand forecasting, (4) improve supplier engagement and distribution/transportation planning. Trade-offs include: higher working capital and inventory cost from building stock, additional pressure on manufacturing capacity, and risk that cutting lead times compromises robustness or is infeasible. Guide toward increasing inventory by ramping up production.

questions.prompt: Present Exhibit 1. The client wants to ramp up production — what does this exhibit tell you?
questions.guidance: Candidate should observe: (1) client has 3 manufacturing locations; (2) total utilization is 100% — all plants run at full capacity; (3) available time splits into production time (~82%), scheduled maintenance (~10%), and unscheduled maintenance (~8%), which is consistent with industry average leaving minimal scope for improvement. Conclusion: capacity is fully constrained, so simply ramping production is not feasible — the client must instead reallocate existing volumes to its most profitable customers.

questions.prompt: How can the client prioritize customers and improve order fulfilment? What information is required?
questions.guidance: Client should prioritize customers by profitability over variable cost per ton, then reallocate limited production capacity to the highest-priority customers. Information needed: revenues, variable costs, volumes ordered, and volumes fulfilled for each customer.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 2, calculate current profitability per customer and rank customers. Then calculate the best-case scenario by reallocating total capacity (127 kt) to the most profitable customers.
questions.guidance: Step 1: calculate volume fulfilled = volume ordered x order fulfilment %. Step 2: calculate profitability/ton = (Revenue / Volume Fulfilled) - 1,250. Step 3: calculate total profitability = profitability/ton x volume fulfilled. Rank by profitability/ton. Observe that high-profitability customers (F, B, G) have low fulfilment rates. Best case: fill F (60 kt), B (45 kt), G (20 kt) to 100% fulfilment = 125 kt; remaining 2 kt goes to C. Total profit rises from 212M to 326M (+54%). Candidate should note that high-value customers are currently under-served.

math.setup: Variable cost = 1,250 EUR/ton. Volume fulfilled = Volume ordered x Order fulfilment %. Profitability/ton = (Revenue_EUR / Volume_fulfilled_tons) - 1,250. Total profit = Profitability/ton x Volume fulfilled. Total capacity = 127 kt (constant).
steps: Current state — Volume fulfilled (kt): A=3, B=27, C=8, D=4, E=19, F=33, G=14, Others=19. Total=127 kt
Current state — Profitability/ton (EUR): A=596, B=2083, C=1250, D=1250, E=350, F=3295, G=1607, Others=63
Current state — Total profit (M EUR): A=2, B=56, C=10, D=5, E=7, F=109, G=23, Others=1. Grand total=212 M EUR
Best case reallocation: Allocate full demand for F=60 kt, B=45 kt, G=20 kt (total=125 kt). Remaining 2 kt goes to C.
Best case — Total profits (M EUR): F=198, B=94, G=32, C=3, D=0, A=0, E=0, Others=0. Grand total=326 M EUR
Profit increase = 326-212 = 114 M EUR, or approximately +54%
math.answer: Best-case total profit = 326 M EUR, up from 212 M EUR, an increase of ~54%. Top 3 customers (F, B, G) achieve 100% order fulfilment.

questions.prompt: What are the risks of focusing only on the top 3 customers, and how can these risks be mitigated?
questions.guidance: Risks should be bucketed into: (1) risks from de-prioritizing other customers — loss of future growth potential from currently smaller customers, customers served at only 20% will likely migrate to competitors; (2) risks from concentration on key customers — volatility or demand drop from F, B, or G, reduced customer diversification. Mitigations: 100% fulfilment may not be necessary — identify each customer's actual expectation and match it; expand capacity via outsourcing or new plant set-up; renegotiate contracts to increase lead time requirements; reduce accepted order sizes; prioritize most crucial product parts; develop differentiated supply chains for different product lines.

brainstorming.prompt: What are some ways the client can increase order fulfilment, and what are the trade-offs of doing that?

categories.name: Reduce lead times
ideas: Streamline manufacturing process steps to cut production time
Reduce transportation time through better carrier selection or warehousing closer to customers
Eliminate non-value-added administrative or handoff delays

categories.name: Increase inventory levels
ideas: Build finished goods safety stock to buffer against demand spikes
Increase raw material inventory to avoid supply disruptions

categories.name: Improve forecasting
ideas: Invest in statistical demand forecasting tools
Collaborate with key customers on forward demand visibility (VMI)
Use historical order patterns to detect seasonality

categories.name: Supplier and logistics improvements
ideas: Strengthen supplier contracts to guarantee on-time raw material delivery

categories.name: Trade-offs
ideas: Higher inventory increases working capital requirements and carrying costs
Ramping production adds pressure on already fully utilized plants
Cutting lead times may compromise process robustness or may not be feasible operationally

recommendation: Undertake a customer prioritization and volume reallocation exercise focusing on the 'Big 3' customers — F, B, and G — which will receive 100% order fulfilment priority, increasing total profits by approximately 54% (from 212 M EUR to 326 M EUR).
Define key customers as those contributing the highest profitability per ton; currently F (3,295 EUR/ton), B (2,083 EUR/ton), and G (1,607 EUR/ton).
Remaining capacity (2 kt) is allocated to the next most profitable customer (C) after Big 3 demand is fully met.
risks: Future growth potential of currently de-prioritized customers may be significant
Customers served at only 20% fulfilment will likely migrate to competitors
Over-reliance on 3 customers creates concentration and volatility risk if any of them reduces orders
next_steps: Implement a weekly process to coordinate volume reallocation and track results against profit and fulfilment targets
Communicate sensitively with the sales team and all customers, especially those being de-prioritized
Explore capacity expansion options (outsourcing, new plant) to eventually serve a broader customer base without trade-offs
Renegotiate contracts with deprioritized customers on realistic lead times or order volumes
